entries.title: Safer saves between devices
items: If you leave Arcline open on one device and play on another, the old tab now notices when it wakes up: it pauses and asks whether to load the newer save, instead of quietly saving its older city over it.

When this device and your account have different saves, each side shows when you really last played it and what's in it (worlds, cities, people). A time the game doesn't know is shown as "not recorded" instead of "just now".
Whenever the account's saves replace this device's, this device's saves are kept as a backup.

entries.title: Bigger blocks, parks and research
items: Zoned land now fills in all the way, middle included: a painted block grows wherever it is within 8 tiles of a road (walking through the same zone), not just along the road. Buildings deeper in face the way out to the street.

Homes, shops and industry now come in three sizes at every level: 1×1, 2×1 and 2×2. Blocks are laid out smartly: a 4×2 strip takes two 2×2 buildings side by side (never one in the middle), and odd widths leave a row of smaller buildings only along one edge.

Small neighbouring buildings combine into one bigger building once they have settled in and the land, power and demand are good enough. Tap a building to see whether its next step is to combine or to go up a level, and what it still needs.

24 new building designs: Pod Court, Garden Duplex, Townhouse, Garden Walk-ups, Slim Apartments, Midrise Bar, Needle Tower and Twin Residences for homes; Kiosk Row, Corner Mart, Corner Shop, Gallery Mall, Studio Offices, Capsule Hotel, Data Spire and Trade Exchange for shops and offices; Fab Shed, Parts Yard, Print Works, Chem Works, Freight Depot, Clean Lab, Drone Assembly and Robot Plant for industry (a new third industry level).

Statistics: open it from the ☰ menu (or press G). Overview gives people, jobs, credits, income per day, power, water, attractiveness, land value and R/C/I demand at a glance. History charts people, credits, income, demand, power and water use against what you make, and attractiveness over the last 30 or 120 days or the whole game. Tap or drag across a chart to read any day. Neighbours lists the cities next door and what each link gives you. Defence shows your turrets, walls and wall health, creatures killed, swarms held and damage taken, with charts.

The world map card now lists a city's neighbours: how each one is linked (road, transit or not yet) and what it gives in numbers: extra home and shop demand, faster move-ins and people a month, plus the total. Transit links show as their own cyan line on the map.
A transit link between two cities now needs a line with a station reaching the shared border on both sides, the same way roads already have to meet.
Cities saved before border roads were recorded keep their road links. The game works them out from the saved city, so you don't have to open and save each one again.
If a neighbour builds a road to your border after you last played, your city now gets a short road to meet it the next time you open it (when the ground there is free), with a message saying so.

New Parks tab (P): 13 new parks and plazas from a Pocket Park, Playground and Fountain Square to a Sports Court, Promenade, Skate Park, Founders' Memorial, Neon Night Plaza, Central Park, Amphitheatre and a Grand Biodome. Each lifts land value around it (the card says how much and how far), pulls in more newcomers while homes sit in its reach, and lights up at night. Holding one shows the Land value view and its reach.

New R&D tab (T): spend credits and materials to research upgrades — stronger pumps and power plants, better drills and refineries, cheaper upkeep, turret Mk II and Mk III refits, tougher walls, new parks, plans that open buildings before their milestone, and city policies you switch on and off. Each card shows what it does in numbers, its price, its time and what it needs. One at a time; stopping gives everything back.

Passing merchants sell many of the same techs, cheaper and at once: an R&D card says when a merchant offers it (and when one is overhead now), and a merchant's offer says which R&D tech it unlocks. Whichever way you get a tech, it's the same one.

The tool bar on phones: icons over short names, arrows and a fade at the ends when there are more tabs, a clear highlight on the open tab, and the map views fold into one View button so nothing covers the tool you're holding.

entries.title: Builder's tools
items: Turrets now point exactly at what they shoot — they used to be turned about 15° off. Creatures face the way they walk more closely too.

Destroyed walls, gates, turrets and buildings leave a see-through ghost. Tap a ghost to rebuild it at its normal price, or use Tools › Bulk repair to rebuild every ghost at once and patch damaged walls — it shows the total first and lets you choose defences, buildings or both.
Undo: Ctrl+Z (or the Undo button at the left of the tool bar) takes back what you just built — a whole road or wall run counts as one — with a full refund, for 60 seconds.
Right-click while dragging a road, wall, power line or zone cancels that drag without building anything; right-click again (or Esc) puts the tool away.

Merchant upgrades now work and show: Mk II and Mk III parts refit every turret of that kind, standing and new, and the build tray, the turret's panel and a message say what changed (Pulse Gun Mk II: 7 → 10 damage a bolt). The wall blueprint, the range blueprint and the landmark discounts now work too.

The build trays show each part's numbers: damage a second and range on turret cards, health on walls, power or water on plants and pumps — and the full list (damage per shot, fire rate, range, power, upkeep) when you hover or select it.

Walls heal themselves a few seconds after the fighting stops, as long as they're above half health. Below half they look cracked and stay damaged until you repair them, so a wall that looks whole really is. Tap a wall to see its health, and a bar shows over walls under attack.
Tap a turret to see its Mk, damage, fire rate and range; tap a wall for its health and a one-tap repair.
Power pylons no longer stand on top of turrets, walls or buildings.
Street lights now line your roads, and most shops and offices put up a neon billboard or a tall glowing sign — the streets light up warmly at night.

Income is shown per day, because that's when you're paid: the Credits box says what the next pay day brings, and a bar under the date (along the Credits box on a phone) fills up to it. The budget lists each line per day too.

Power and Water turn amber when you're close to using all you make and red when you're over, with a message the moment it happens. Tap Power, Water or the R/C/I bars for a sheet: what you use and make, which buildings are short, what to build, and why each zone wants more or less.

Tap a home, shop or workshop to see how close it is to its next level and what it still needs — land value, water, power, room to grow, more demand. Buildings now really do level up when they're ready, growing into the zoned land beside them.
Bridges sit level with their banks instead of dipping below the ground.

Roads between neighbouring cities: when you open a new region next to one of your cities, it starts with a short road wherever your other city's road reaches the border, so the two line up. The world map shows a link only where both cities' roads meet.
Opening a new region no longer shows cars left over from your last city.

entries.title: Tidier streets
items: Cars, haulers and trams now drive straight along their lanes and take corners squarely, instead of looking like they were sliding sideways down the road.

Terrace homes and shop rows always turn their fronts to the street and stay on their own lot — they no longer stick out into the road or into the houses next door. Cities you have already built are fixed when you load them.
Fixed: the music could stumble after you switched to another tab and came back.

entries.title: Music and a city you can hear
items: Arcline has its own music: synthwave that plays itself and keeps changing — a calm theme while you build, a dreamier one at night, and a driving one when a swarm is announced or the walls are under attack. It drops for a moment under a big blast.

Zoom out and the fighting gets quieter while the city takes over: traffic and the hum of machinery, wind over the wilds, alien birds by day and alien insects at night, and rain or storms when the weather turns. Zoom in on a fight and the guns are as loud as ever. Fights off screen are quieter too.
Settings has separate sliders for Music, Effects and Ambience, as well as the main volume and Mute.
Rivers now sit below their banks — wide rivers were drawn raised up on a ledge.
Right-click cancels the build and bulldoze tools.
New cities start with 35,000 credits (was 60,000): money is tighter at the start.
Roofs and their tanks and antennas sit on their own wing of a building, and the darkest building style is gone from the city.

entries.title: A city that grows
items: People now move in on their own whenever there are free homes — more when the city is attractive (land value, jobs, power, water, low taxes) and fewer just after a wall breaks. Hover the people counter to see why.
A colony grant pays the bills while your city is small, and upkeep is lower, so a well-built town makes money from the first months.
Drop pods now bring supply crates: a free one from the colony's sponsors every few weeks, and anything you buy from merchants.

Power lines: draw a line and the pylons place themselves, evenly spaced with wires between them. Power reaches nearby buildings, and zones and buildings pass it on — the Power view shows where it reaches.
Roads can run through walls: a road across a wall becomes a gate. Build roads to the region edge to link up with a neighbouring city — linked cities grow faster.
Tap a building you placed to move it: free for the first minute, then 10% of its price.
The Comms panel (C, or tap a Comms Array) shows ships overhead, the schedule of merchant convoys and warship patrols, and lets you call one in.
The wildlife never runs out: new nests move in from beyond the region, and creatures go for gates before walls.
Your cities appear on the world map as they really look.
Fixed: the New world button on phones, and a stray light on the Colony Core.

entries.title: First landing
items: Make a whole planet: name it, pick its size and how fierce the wildlife is, and watch the map change as you go. The world map shows every region side by side in small, medium and large sizes.
Pick a region and a landing spot: the founding ship drops your Colony Core and the first settlers in a rain of pods.
Lay streets, avenues and highways, zone homes, shops and industry, and watch the city grow — from pod homes to towers and hotels as land value rises.
Run power and water (with an underground view for pipes), build schools, parks and an arena, and keep the budget in the black with taxes for each zone.
People arrive by ship: build a Comms Array and answer the ships passing overhead — settlers, warships selling orbital strikes, and merchants with rare goods.
Alien wildlife never stops probing: wall off the wilds, put Pulse Guns, Mortars, Arc Coils and Rail Lances behind the wall, repair what they chew, and call down an orbital strike on a swarm.
Mine Metal, Stone and Crystal at outposts and refine them into Steel, Concrete and Power cells for the big buildings.
Rain, thunderstorms, auroras and shooting stars, a day and night cycle where the city lights up, and traffic on the roads.
Your worlds are saved in this browser. Sign in to keep them on your account and carry them to another device.
